title: Bundle Adjustment & Nonlinear Optimization
blurb: Nonlinear least squares done properly: Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt, the reprojection error, the sparse Jacobian of bundle adjustment, the Schur complement that makes it tractable, and the constrained-optimisation identities that keep reappearing.

knowledge_points.title: Quadratic Approximation, Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt
knowledge_points.recap:
**Setting.** Minimise $f(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2$ with a differentiable residual $r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$.
**Second-order Taylor of $f$.** At $x=x_0+\Delta x$:
$$f(x)\approx f(x_0)+\nabla f(x_0)^\top\Delta x+\tfrac12\Delta x^\top H(x_0)\Delta x.$$
**First-order Taylor of $r$** instead (this is the Gauss–Newton idea):
$$f(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2\approx\|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\|_2^2=\|r(x_0)\|_2^2+2r(x_0)^\top J_r\Delta x+\|J_r\Delta x\|_2^2.$$
Matching terms with the Taylor expansion identifies the **approximate Hessian**
$$H\approx2J_r^\top J_r,$$
i.e. second derivatives of $r$ are dropped. Note $J_r^\top J_r$ is **not** the Hessian of $r$ — it is an approximation of the Hessian of $f$.
**The two update problems.**
$$\text{Gauss–Newton:}\quad\min_{\Delta x}\ \|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\|_2^2,$$
$$\text{Levenberg–Marquardt:}\quad\min_{\Delta x}\ \|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\|_2^2+\lambda\|D\Delta x\|_2^2,$$
with a diagonal $D$ and weight $\lambda$. Solving them gives $\Delta x=-(J^\top J)^{-1}J^\top r$ and $\Delta x=-(J^\top J+\lambda D^\top D)^{-1}J^\top r$.
**Role of $\lambda$.** $\lambda\to0$ ⇒ pure Gauss–Newton (large, fast steps). $\lambda\to\infty$ ⇒ the step becomes small and aligns with the **negative gradient** — a trust region. High $\lambda$ therefore keeps $\Delta x$ small and **stabilises the inversion** when $J^\top J$ is (near-)singular: $J^\top J+\lambda D^\top D$ is positive definite, hence invertible, for any $\lambda>0$ with $D$ of full rank.
**Both are iterative** and both find only a **local** minimum — never a guaranteed global one, and not a saddle point.
**Newton's method** uses the exact Hessian; Gauss–Newton is an *approximation of Newton*, not the other way round. Newton needs an invertible Hessian, so it cannot be applied to every problem. On a quadratic it converges in **one** step: for $\min(x-2)^2$ with $\gamma=1$ from $x_0=-2$, one Newton step lands exactly on $x=2$.
**1D Gauss–Newton.** For $E(x)=r(x)^2$ the step is
$$\Delta_t=-r(x_t)\big(r'(x_t)\big)^{-1}$$
— the Newton step on $r$ itself. Examples from $x_0=2$: $r(x)=x^2$ gives $\Delta=-x/2$, so $2\to1\to\tfrac12$ (halving, never reaching 0); $r(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)|x|^{1/3}$ gives $\Delta=-3x$, so $2\to-4\to8$ (**divergence**); $r(x)=\max(x,2x-1)$ gives $\Delta=-r/2$ on the linear piece, so $2\to\tfrac12\to0$ (**finite convergence**).
**2023 paper focus.** Steepest descent is the method prone to zig-zagging. Newton uses the true Hessian and a second-order model of the objective; Gauss–Newton linearises residuals and substitutes $J^\top J$, avoiding residual second derivatives.
**Diagonal LM damping.** A common variant uses $(J^\top J+\lambda\operatorname{diag}(J^\top J))\Delta=-J^\top r$ rather than $\lambda I$. Keep the Jacobian factor on the right; simplifying is safe only after checking symmetry and invertibility.

questions.q: With $r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ differentiable, when optimising $f(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2$ a common approach is to approximate the function locally by a quadratic. What does the quadratic approximation of $f(x)$ for $x=x_0+\Delta x$ look like if we apply the Taylor expansion of $f(x)$ at $x_0$? Express it in terms of the Hessian $H$, the gradient $\nabla f$ and the function value $f$ at $x_0$.
questions.answer:
$$f(x)\approx f(x_0)+\nabla f(x_0)^\top\Delta x+\tfrac12\Delta x^\top H(x_0)\Delta x.$$
**Reading.** This is the standard second-order Taylor expansion: a constant, a linear term from the gradient, and a quadratic term from the Hessian — all evaluated at the current iterate $x_0$.
questions.extend: Note the $\tfrac12$ on the Hessian term; forgetting it propagates a factor 2 into the identification $H\approx2J^\top J$ later.

questions.q: What does the quadratic approximation of $f(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2$ look like if we apply the **first-order** Taylor expansion of $r(x)$ at $x_0$? Express it in terms of the residual $r$ and the Jacobian $J_r$ at $x_0$. By identifying terms with the previous answer: what is the approximation of the Hessian $H$ of $f$?
questions.answer:
$$f(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2\approx\|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\|_2^2=\|r(x_0)\|_2^2+2r(x_0)^\top J_r\Delta x+\|J_r\Delta x\|_2^2.$$
**Identifying terms** with $f(x_0)+\nabla f^\top\Delta x+\tfrac12\Delta x^\top H\Delta x$: the linear term gives $\nabla f=2J_r^\top r(x_0)$, and the quadratic term $\|J_r\Delta x\|^2=\Delta x^\top J_r^\top J_r\Delta x$ gives
$$H\approx2J_r^\top J_r.$$
**Meaning.** The second derivatives of $r$ are discarded — cheap, and accurate when the residual is small or nearly linear.
questions.extend: $J_r^\top J_r$ approximates the Hessian **of $f$**, not of $r$. Calling it "the Hessian of the residual function" is a marked-wrong MC option.

questions.q: When optimising $f(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2$ with a general nonlinear $r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$, state the two optimisation problems whose solutions give the update step of the Gauss–Newton and the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm respectively. Use a diagonal matrix $D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and weight $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ for the regularisation term.
questions.answer:
**Gauss–Newton:**
$$\min_{\Delta x}\ \big\|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\big\|_2^2.$$
**Levenberg–Marquardt:**
$$\min_{\Delta x}\ \big\|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\big\|_2^2+\lambda\|D\Delta x\|_2^2.$$
**Difference.** LM adds a damping / trust-region term that penalises large steps; solving the normal equations gives $\Delta x=-(J^\top J)^{-1}J^\top r$ and $\Delta x=-(J^\top J+\lambda D^\top D)^{-1}J^\top r$ respectively.

questions.q: Are the Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt methods iterative optimisation algorithms?
questions.answer: **Yes, both are iterative optimisation algorithms.** Each computes a local linearisation at the current estimate, takes a step, and repeats until convergence — neither produces a closed-form solution.

questions.q: Using the notation of the previous questions, which of the following is correct?
questions.answer:
**For high values of $\lambda$, the update step $\Delta x$ will be small — we stay in the trust region.**
**Why.** The damping term $\lambda\|D\Delta x\|^2$ penalises large steps, so increasing $\lambda$ shrinks $\Delta x$; in the limit the step direction also tends towards the negative gradient.
**Why the others fail.** For high $\lambda$ with $D=I$ the step **does** approach the gradient direction (the first option states the opposite). The regularisation **does** help to stabilise the inversion — $J^\top J+\lambda D^\top D$ is positive definite for $\lambda>0$. And $J_r^\top J_r$ approximates the Hessian of $f$, **not** the Hessian of the residual function $r$.

options.text: For high values of $\lambda$, and $D$ the identity, the update step will not become closer to the direction of the gradient of $\|r(x)\|^2$.
For high values of $\lambda$, the update step $\Delta x$ will be small, we stay in the trust region.
The regularisation does not help to stabilise the computation of the inverse of $J_r^\top J_r$.
The term $J_r^\top J_r$ is the Hessian of the residual function $r$.

questions.q: Are we guaranteed to find the global minimum of $f(x)$ when using the Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm?
questions.answer:
**No — the algorithms only find a local minimum.**
**Why.** Both are local descent methods based on a linearisation around the current iterate. On a non-convex problem (and bundle adjustment is non-convex) the result depends on the initialisation, which is precisely why a linear algorithm such as the eight-point algorithm is used to initialise.
**Not a saddle point.** With a proper line search / damping the methods converge to a local **minimum**, not to a saddle.

options.text: No, the algorithms only find a local minimum.
No, the algorithms only find a saddle point.
Yes, the algorithms always find the global minimum.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true?
questions.answer:
**Newton's method applied to $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}(x-2)^2$ with step size $\gamma=1$ and initialisation $x_0=-2$ converges to the global minimum in one step.**
**Why.** The objective is exactly quadratic, so its second-order Taylor expansion is exact and one Newton step jumps straight to the vertex $x=2$.
**Why the others fail.** **Gauss–Newton is an approximation of Newton's method**, not the reverse. There **are** non-convex problems solvable to global optimality (e.g. many with hidden convexity or closed-form spectral solutions). Gauss–Newton is for **unconstrained** least squares and cannot be applied directly to a constrained problem. And Newton's method needs an invertible Hessian, so it cannot be applied to *any* optimisation problem.

options.text: Newton's method is an approximation of the Gauss-Newton algorithm
There are no non-convex optimisation problems that can be solved to global optimality
Newton's method applied to $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}(x-2)^2$, with step size $\gamma=1$ and initialisation $x_0=-2$, converges to the problem's global minimum in 1 step
The Gauss-Newton algorithm can be directly applied to solve a constrained optimisation problem
Newton's method can be applied to solve any optimisation problem
None of the other options

questions.q: The Gauss–Newton method is used to minimise $E(x)=(r(x))^2$ with $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $r:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$. One step is $x_{t+1}=x_t+\Delta_t$, at points where $r'(x_t)$ is defined, $r(x_t)\neq0$ and $r'(x_t)\neq0$. What is the correct expression for $\Delta_t$?
questions.answer:
$$\Delta_t=-r(x_t)\big(r'(x_t)\big)^{-1}.$$
**Derivation.** In one dimension the Jacobian is $J=r'(x_t)$, so the Gauss–Newton step $\Delta=-(J^\top J)^{-1}J^\top r$ becomes $-\big(r'(x_t)^2\big)^{-1}r'(x_t)r(x_t)=-\dfrac{r(x_t)}{r'(x_t)}$.
**Recognise it.** This is exactly Newton's root-finding step applied to $r$ — Gauss–Newton on a squared residual drives the residual itself to zero.
questions.extend: Residual in the numerator, derivative in the denominator. The decoys swap them or square the wrong factor.

options.text: $\Delta_t=-r'(x_t)\big(r(x_t)\big)^{-1}$
$\Delta_t=-r(x_t)\big(r'(x_t)\big)^{-2}$
$\Delta_t=-r'(x_t)\big(r(x_t)\big)^{-2}$
$\Delta_t=-r(x_t)\big(r'(x_t)\big)^{-1}$

questions.q: Gauss–Newton is applied to $E(x)=r(x)^2$ from $x_0=2$ with $r_1(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)|x|^{1/3}$, $r_2(x)=x^2$, $r_3(x)=\max(x,2x-1)$. Match each residual to its step sequence: **A**: $2,1,\tfrac12$; **B**: $2,-4,8$; **C**: $2,\tfrac12,0$.
questions.answer:
Using $\Delta_t=-r(x_t)/r'(x_t)$:
**$r_1(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)|x|^{1/3}$ → sequence B ($2,-4,8$).** Here $r'=\tfrac13|x|^{-2/3}$, so $\Delta=-\dfrac{|x|^{1/3}}{\tfrac13|x|^{-2/3}}=-3x$, giving $x_{t+1}=x_t-3x_t=-2x_t$: $2\to-4\to8$ — the iterates **diverge**, doubling in magnitude and alternating sign.
**$r_2(x)=x^2$ → sequence A ($2,1,\tfrac12$).** $\Delta=-\dfrac{x^2}{2x}=-\dfrac{x}{2}$, so $x_{t+1}=\tfrac{x_t}{2}$: $2\to1\to\tfrac12$ — halving, converging to $0$ but never reaching it.
**$r_3(x)=\max(x,2x-1)$ → sequence C ($2,\tfrac12,0$).** For $x>1$ the active branch is $2x-1$ with $r'=2$, so $\Delta=-\tfrac{2x-1}{2}$ and $x_1=2-\tfrac32=\tfrac12$. For $x<1$ the branch is $x$ with $r'=1$, so $\Delta=-x$ and $x_2=0$ — **exact convergence in two steps** once a linear piece is active.
**Lesson.** Gauss–Newton converges in one step on a linear residual, converges slowly on a flat-minimum residual, and **diverges** when the residual has infinite slope at the root.
questions.extend: A cube-root residual has $r'\to\infty$ at the root, which makes the Newton step overshoot by a constant factor — the textbook divergence example.

questions.q: Let $r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ with Jacobian $J_r$, and consider $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2$. State the name of the algorithm whose update is $x^{(k+1)}=\arg\min_{x}\tfrac12(x-x^{(k)})^\top J_r^\top J_r(x-x^{(k)})+(x-x^{(k)})^\top J_r^\top r$, with $r,J_r$ evaluated at $x^{(k)}$.
questions.answer:
**Gauss–Newton.**
**Why.** The expression is exactly the expansion of $\tfrac12\|r(x^{(k)})+J_r(x-x^{(k)})\|^2$ up to a constant: the quadratic term uses the **approximate** Hessian $J_r^\top J_r$ and the linear term the gradient $J_r^\top r$. Adding a damping term $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|D(x-x^{(k)})\|^2$ would turn it into Levenberg–Marquardt.

questions.q: (a) Derive the Gauss–Newton update step by minimising the linearised cost. (b) When can $J^\top J$ be singular and what goes wrong in practice? (c) Derive the Levenberg–Marquardt update, state what happens as $\lambda\to0$ and $\lambda\to\infty$, and explain why $J^\top J+\lambda D^\top D$ is always invertible for $\lambda>0$ with $D$ of full rank.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Minimise $\|r+J\Delta x\|^2=r^\top r+2r^\top J\Delta x+\Delta x^\top J^\top J\Delta x$. Setting the gradient $2J^\top r+2J^\top J\Delta x$ to zero gives the normal equations $J^\top J\Delta x=-J^\top r$, hence
$$\Delta x=-(J^\top J)^{-1}J^\top r.$$
**(b)** $J^\top J$ is singular exactly when $J$ does not have full column rank — i.e. when some parameter direction does not affect the residual (gauge freedom: the global similarity of a reconstruction, an unobserved landmark, a degenerate configuration). In practice the linear solve blows up or produces enormous, meaningless steps, and near-singularity makes the step direction extremely noise-sensitive.
**(c)** Adding $\lambda\|D\Delta x\|^2$ gives $(J^\top J+\lambda D^\top D)\Delta x=-J^\top r$. As $\lambda\to0$ this becomes pure Gauss–Newton (large steps, fast near the optimum); as $\lambda\to\infty$ the step tends to $-\tfrac{1}{\lambda}(D^\top D)^{-1}J^\top r$, i.e. a **small step along the negative gradient** — gradient descent with a tiny step. Invertibility: $J^\top J\succeq0$ always, and $\lambda D^\top D\succ0$ for $\lambda>0$ with $D$ full rank; the sum of a positive semi-definite and a positive definite matrix is positive definite, hence invertible.
questions.extend: LM is the interpolation between the two classical extremes: trust the model ($\lambda$ small, Gauss–Newton) or trust only the slope ($\lambda$ large, gradient descent).

questions.q: Let $g(\Delta x)=\|r(x_0)+J_r\Delta x\|_2^2$ approximate $f$ locally at $x_0$, with gradient $\nabla g=J_r^\top r(x_0)+J_r^\top J_r\Delta x$. Compute the gradient of the objective when the Levenberg–Marquardt regulariser $\lambda\|D\Delta x\|_2^2$ is present, and state the update step.
questions.answer:
**Gradient with the regulariser.** Differentiating $\lambda\|D\Delta x\|_2^2=\lambda\Delta x^\top D^\top D\Delta x$ adds $\lambda D^\top D\Delta x$ (up to the same factor convention), so
$$\nabla g+\lambda D^\top D\Delta x=J_r^\top r(x_0)+J_r^\top J_r\Delta x+\lambda D^\top D\Delta x.$$
**Update step.** Setting the gradient to zero and solving for $\Delta x$:
$$\Delta x=-\big(J_r^\top J_r+\lambda D^\top D\big)^{-1}J_r^\top r(x_0).$$
**Sanity check.** With $\lambda=0$ this reduces to the Gauss–Newton step $\Delta x=-(J_r^\top J_r)^{-1}J_r^\top r$; as $\lambda\to\infty$ the step shrinks and turns towards $-J_r^\top r$, the negative gradient direction.
questions.extend: The damping enters **only** in the matrix to be inverted, never in the right-hand side — that is what guarantees invertibility without changing the descent direction at $\lambda=0$.

questions.q: Iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) is used for $E(x)=\sum_i w_i(x)\,|a_i-f_i(x)|^2$. (a) Write the IRLS update. (b) If $f_i(x)=b_i^\top x$, derive the weighted normal equations for one iteration. (c) Why does solving every subproblem exactly not guarantee a global minimum of $E$?
questions.answer:
**(a)** Freeze the weights at the current estimate and solve
$$x_{t+1}=\arg\min_x\sum_i w_i(x_t)\,|a_i-f_i(x)|^2.$$
**(b)** With $A$ containing rows $b_i^\top$, observation vector $a$, and $W_t=\operatorname{diag}(w_i(x_t))$, the subproblem is $\min_x\|W_t^{1/2}(a-Ax)\|^2$. Its normal equations are
$$A^\top W_tA\,x_{t+1}=A^\top W_ta,$$
so $x_{t+1}=(A^\top W_tA)^{-1}A^\top W_ta$ when the matrix is invertible.
**(c)** Although each frozen-weight problem is quadratic, the weights depend on $x$, so the original objective is generally **non-convex**. IRLS is iterative and initialization-dependent; it can converge to a local minimum or stationary point rather than the global minimum.
questions.extend: The weights are evaluated at $x_t$, not at the unknown $x_{t+1}$; otherwise the subproblem would not be an ordinary weighted least-squares solve.

questions.q:
Let $F(x)=\frac12\|r(x)\|^2$.

1. Derive the exact gradient and Hessian. (4)
2. Identify the term omitted by Gauss-Newton. (2)
3. Derive the Gauss-Newton update and state two situations in which the approximation is accurate. (3)
questions.answer:
For $F(x)=\tfrac12\sum_i r_i(x)^2$,
$$\nabla F=J^\top r,\qquad \nabla^2F=J^\top J+\sum_i r_i\nabla^2r_i.$$
Gauss--Newton drops the residual-weighted second-derivative term and solves
$$J^\top J\,\Delta x=-J^\top r.$$
The approximation is accurate near a well-fitting solution where residuals are small, or when the residual functions are nearly linear so their second derivatives are small.
questions.extend: Generated set Q47-B: From Newton to Gauss-Newton (9 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Which statements about non-linear optimisation are **wrong**?
questions.answer: **Wrong: 2, 3 and 4.** Steepest descent follows the negative gradient. Its poor scaling is what commonly causes zig-zagging. Newton uses the true Hessian and a second-order Taylor model of the objective; Gauss-Newton linearises residuals and uses $J^\top J$ as a Hessian approximation, usually avoiding the expensive second-derivative terms.

options.text: Steepest descent moves along the negative-gradient direction at each iteration.
Newton's method is more prone to a zig-zag trajectory than steepest descent.
Gauss-Newton is more time-consuming than Newton because Gauss-Newton must compute the Hessian.
Newton and Gauss-Newton both use a second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function.

questions.q: For symmetric positive-definite $A$ and residual $r(x)=Ax+b$, write the Levenberg–Marquardt update used in the official solution for minimising $\langle Ax+b,Ax+b\rangle$.
questions.answer: With $J_r=A$, the diagonal-damped LM step is $\Delta=-(A^\top A+\lambda\operatorname{diag}(A^\top A))^{-1}A^\top(Ax+b)$. Since $A^\top=A$, this is equivalently $\Delta=- ig(A+A^{-1}\lambda\operatorname{diag}(A^2) ig)^{-1}(Ax+b)$.

knowledge_points.title: Bundle Adjustment: Energy, Properties and the Jacobian
knowledge_points.recap:
**What it minimises.** Bundle adjustment minimises the **(re-)projection error** — Euclidean distances between observed and projected image points. Contrast: **direct image alignment** minimises the **photometric error** (intensity differences); the **eight-point algorithm** minimises **neither** (it minimises an algebraic residual).
**Two-view energy.**
$$E(R,T,X^1,\dots,X^N)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\big\|\tilde x_1^j-\pi(X^j)\big\|^2+\big\|\tilde x_2^j-\pi(R,T,X^j)\big\|^2.$$
This is an **indirect** (feature-based) approach: it compares *geometric* positions, not intensities.
$\pi(R,T,X^j)$ first transforms $X^j$ into the frame of camera 2 via $\lambda x=RX^j+T$ and then projects, i.e. takes the first two components of the right-hand side divided by the third (no $K$ in normalised coordinates). The first term has no pose parameters because the **world frame is chosen to coincide with camera 1** — an active modelling choice, not a necessity.
**Properties (a recurring MC block).** Bundle adjustment: jointly estimates structure **and** motion; is **non-convex**; **requires initialisation** (typically from a linear algorithm); can be formulated for different noise models; and has **no closed-form solution** — it is minimised by nonlinear least-squares algorithms. Also: **direct** methods give a *dense* or semi-dense reconstruction, not a sparse one, and tend to be more robust in low-texture regions.
**Projective bundle adjustment.** Instead of $SE(3)$ poses plus known $K$ (metric reconstruction), one can optimise full $3\times4$ projective camera matrices $P_i$ — an **unconstrained projective** reconstruction, appropriate for **uncalibrated** structure-from-motion.
**Sizes (worth practising).** With $n_c$ cameras, $n_l$ landmarks and every camera seeing every landmark: residual $r\in\mathbb{R}^{2n_cn_l}$; camera Jacobian $J_p\in\mathbb{R}^{2n_cn_l\times12n_c}$ (12 entries per $P_i$); landmark Jacobian $J_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{2n_cn_l\times3n_l}$ (3 unknowns per $X_j$, the homogeneous coordinate being fixed). E.g. 10 cameras, 100 landmarks ⇒ $r\in\mathbb{R}^{2000}$, $J_p\in\mathbb{R}^{2000\times120}$, $J_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{2000\times300}$, $J\in\mathbb{R}^{2000\times420}$.
**Sparsity.** Residual $r_{ij}$ depends only on camera $i$ and landmark $j$, so each row block of $J_p$ has non-zeros in **one** camera block and each row block of $J_\ell$ in **one** landmark block. That block-sparsity is what the Schur complement exploits.
**Linear initializer versus nonlinear refinement.** The eight-point algorithm minimises an algebraic epipolar residual and is mainly an initializer. Bundle adjustment minimises summed pixel reprojection errors $\|\tilde x-\pi(RX+T)\|^2$ jointly over poses and structure; with robust losses and a good initialisation it handles noise and outliers much better.

questions.q: Which statement about **Bundle Adjustment** is true?
questions.answer:
**Bundle Adjustment minimises the (re-)projection error** — the Euclidean distances between observed image points and the projections of the estimated 3D points.
**Contrast the three classics.** *Direct image alignment* minimises the **photometric** error (intensity differences). *Bundle adjustment* minimises the **reprojection** error. The *eight-point algorithm* minimises **neither** — only an algebraic residual.
questions.extend: Geometric error ⇒ bundle adjustment. Photometric error ⇒ direct methods. Algebraic error ⇒ linear (eight-point) algorithms.

options.text: Bundle Adjustment minimises the (re-)projection error (Euclidean point distances).
Bundle Adjustment minimises neither the (re-)projection error nor the photometric error.
Bundle Adjustment minimises the photometric error (intensity differences).

questions.q: Which statement about **Direct Image Alignment** is true?
questions.answer:
**Direct Image Alignment minimises the photometric error** (intensity differences between corresponding pixels).
**Why.** Direct methods skip feature extraction entirely and optimise pose and geometry so that the warped image intensities match — the residual is $I_2(w(x,\xi))-I_1(x)$, not a point distance.

options.text: Direct Image Alignment minimises the (re-)projection error (Euclidean point distances).
Direct Image Alignment minimises neither the (re-)projection error nor the photometric error.
Direct Image Alignment minimises the photometric error (intensity differences).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about bundle adjustment is **wrong**?
questions.answer:
**Wrong:** "The bundle adjustment problem can be solved in closed form."
**Why.** Bundle adjustment is a difficult **non-convex** problem for which no closed-form solution is known; it is solved iteratively by nonlinear least-squares algorithms (Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt).
**All the others are true.** It can be defined for different noise models; it is non-convex; it can estimate structure and motion **simultaneously**; it **requires initialisation**; and a linear algorithm (e.g. the eight-point algorithm) is the standard way to provide that initialisation.

options.text: We can define bundle adjustment for different noise models
Bundle adjustment is a non-convex problem
The bundle adjustment problem can be solved in closed-form
Bundle adjustment can estimate structure and motion simultaneously
Bundle adjustment requires initialisation
We can use a linear algorithm to initialise bundle adjustment

questions.q: Which of the following statements is **wrong**?
questions.answer:
**Wrong:** "Direct methods provide a sparse geometric reconstruction of the scene."
**Why.** Direct methods operate on image intensities over (semi-)dense pixel sets, so they yield a **dense or semi-dense** reconstruction. It is the *indirect*, feature-based pipeline (keypoints + bundle adjustment) that produces a **sparse** point cloud.
**The others are true.** Bundle-adjustment-type costs are minimised by nonlinear least-squares algorithms; bundle adjustment jointly estimates pose and landmark updates; it needs initialisation; and direct methods, using all the photometric information rather than a few keypoints, tend to be more robust to noise and low texture.
questions.extend: Direct ⇒ dense/semi-dense, photometric. Indirect ⇒ sparse, geometric. Do not swap them.

options.text: Bundle adjustment type cost functions are typically minimised by nonlinear least squares algorithms
Bundle adjustment jointly estimates the pose and the landmark updates
Direct methods provide a sparse geometric reconstruction of the scene
Bundle adjustment problem needs to be initialised
Direct methods tend to be more robust to noise

questions.q: Consider the two-view bundle adjustment energy $E(R,T,X^1,\dots,X^N)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|\tilde x_1^j-\pi(X^j)\|^2+\|\tilde x_2^j-\pi(R,T,X^j)\|^2$ in normalised coordinates. (a) Does it define a **direct** approach? (b) What does $\pi(R,T,X^j)$ represent, and what steps evaluate it? (c) Why does $\pi(X^j)$ not depend on the pose parameters?
questions.answer:
**(a) No — it is an indirect approach.** A direct approach would compare **image intensities**; this energy minimises a **geometric** error (the reprojection error between observed and projected feature positions).
**(b)** $\pi(R,T,X^j)$ first **transforms** the point $X^j$ into the coordinate system of camera 2 and then **projects** it onto the image plane. Concretely, from
$$\lambda x=RX^j+T,$$
the result is the first two components of the right-hand side divided by its third component. (No intrinsics $K$ appears because we work in normalised coordinates.)
**(c)** Because the **world coordinate system is chosen to coincide with camera 1**, i.e. the $X^j$ are already expressed in the first camera's frame, so no coordinate transform is needed before projecting into image 1.
*Remark:* the world frame need not coincide with camera 1 — that is an active modelling choice which produces exactly this form of the energy.
questions.extend: Fixing the world frame to camera 1 also fixes the gauge freedom of the problem — otherwise $J^\top J$ would be singular by construction.

questions.q: In projective bundle adjustment the residual is $r_{ij}=\Pi(P_i,X_j)-m_{ij}$ with $P_i\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}$ and $X_j\in\mathbb{R}^4$ homogeneous. What is the difference between these residuals and those of traditional bundle adjustment? In which practical situations should the projective formulation be used?
questions.answer:
**Traditional bundle adjustment.** Poses are parameterised by $SE(3)$ and the intrinsics $K$ are known, giving a **metric** reconstruction (correct up to a similarity).
**Here.** The full $3\times4$ **projective camera matrices** are optimised directly, with no constraint tying them to a rotation, translation and calibration — an **unconstrained projective** reconstruction.
**Use case.** **Uncalibrated structure-from-motion** / projective bundle adjustment: when the intrinsics are unknown, one first recovers a projective reconstruction and later upgrades it to metric via self-calibration.

questions.q: With 10 cameras, 100 landmarks and every camera seeing every landmark, what is the dimension of the residual vector $r$ and of the Jacobian $J=[J_p\ \ J_\ell]$, where $J_p$ is w.r.t. all camera matrices $\{P_i\}$ and $J_\ell$ w.r.t. all landmarks $\{X_j\}$?
questions.answer:
**Residual vector.** Each observation contributes a $2$-vector, and there are $10\times100=1000$ observations:
$$r\in\mathbb{R}^{2\cdot10\cdot100}=\mathbb{R}^{2000}.$$
**Camera Jacobian.** $10$ cameras $\times$ $12$ entries per $3\times4$ matrix $=120$ unknowns:
$$J_p\in\mathbb{R}^{2000\times120}.$$
**Landmark Jacobian.** $100$ landmarks $\times$ $3$ unknowns each (the homogeneous coordinate is fixed to 1):
$$J_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{2000\times300}.$$
**Full Jacobian.** $J=[J_p\ \ J_\ell]\in\mathbb{R}^{2000\times420}$.
questions.extend: Rows = 2 × observations. Columns = parameters. The landmark count uses 3, not 4 — the fourth homogeneous coordinate is not a free unknown.

questions.q: Derive the per-observation Jacobians $J^{(p)}_{ij}=\frac{\partial r_{ij}}{\partial\operatorname{vec}(P_i)}$ and $J^{(\ell)}_{ij}=\frac{\partial r_{ij}}{\partial X_j}$ for $\Pi(P_i,X_j)=\big(\tfrac{P_{i,0:}X_j}{P_{i,2:}X_j},\ \tfrac{P_{i,1:}X_j}{P_{i,2:}X_j}\big)^\top$.
questions.answer:
Write the rows of $P_i$ as $p_0,p_1,p_2\in\mathbb{R}^4$ and set $x_c=p_0\!\cdot\!X_j$, $y_c=p_1\!\cdot\!X_j$, $z_c=p_2\!\cdot\!X_j$, so $\Pi=(x_c/z_c,\ y_c/z_c)^\top$.
**W.r.t. the landmark** (3 unknowns, since the last coordinate of $X_j$ is fixed), by the quotient rule:
$$J^{(\ell)}_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{p_0^{(xyz)}z_c-p_2^{(xyz)}x_c}{z_c^2}\\[2mm]\dfrac{p_1^{(xyz)}z_c-p_2^{(xyz)}y_c}{z_c^2}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times3},$$
where $p_k^{(xyz)}$ denotes the first three components of row $p_k$.
**W.r.t. the camera** (12 vectorised entries):
$$J^{(p)}_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial p_0}&\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial p_1}&\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial p_2}\\[2mm]\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial p_0}&\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial p_1}&\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial p_2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}X_j^\top/z_c&0&-x_cX_j^\top/z_c^2\\0&X_j^\top/z_c&-y_cX_j^\top/z_c^2\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times12}.$$
The three blocks correspond to the derivatives w.r.t. $p_0$, $p_1$ and $p_2$ respectively.
questions.extend: Every entry carries a $1/z_c$ or $1/z_c^2$ — the quotient rule on the perspective division. That $1/z^2$ is also why points near $z_c\approx0$ destabilise bundle adjustment.

questions.q: In the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm, how is the approximate Hessian of the minimisation problem associated with the residual $r$ expressed in terms of the Jacobian $J$?
questions.answer:
$$H\approx J^\top J+\lambda\operatorname{diag}(J^\top J)=\begin{pmatrix}J_p^\top J_p&J_p^\top J_\ell\\J_\ell^\top J_p&J_\ell^\top J_\ell\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\operatorname{diag}(\cdot).$$
**Reading the blocks.** $J_p^\top J_p$ couples cameras with cameras, $J_\ell^\top J_\ell$ landmarks with landmarks (block-**diagonal**, since each landmark is independent given the cameras), and the off-diagonal $J_p^\top J_\ell$ couples the two. That structure is exactly what the Schur complement exploits.

questions.q: In bundle adjustment the Jacobian is $J=[J_p\ \ J_\ell]$. Why are $J_p$ and $J_\ell$ sparse? Describe their sparsity pattern.
questions.answer:
**Reason.** The residual $r_{ij}$ of observation $(i,j)$ depends **only** on camera $i$ and landmark $j$ — the projection of one point into one image involves no other parameter.
**Pattern.** In the row block belonging to $r_{ij}$: $J_p$ has non-zeros only in the $12$ (or $6$) columns of camera $i$, and $J_\ell$ only in the $3$ columns of landmark $j$; everything else is zero. So both are **block-sparse**, with exactly one non-zero block per row block.
**Consequence for $J^\top J$.** $J_\ell^\top J_\ell$ is **block-diagonal** with $3\times3$ blocks (landmarks do not interact directly), and $J_p^\top J_\ell$ has a non-zero block only where camera $i$ actually observes landmark $j$ — the visibility pattern of the dataset. Real problems observe each landmark in only a handful of images, so the density is very low.
questions.extend: Sparsity is not an optimisation nicety here — a dense solve on $10^5$ landmarks is impossible, so exploiting it is what makes bundle adjustment run at all.

questions.q: A separable least-squares problem has nonlinear pose variables $p$ and linear structure variables $\ell$: $E(p,\ell)=\|A(p)\ell-b\|_2^2$. (a) Eliminate $\ell$ by variable projection and write the reduced problem in $p$. (b) How does this idea help projective bundle adjustment, and how is it conceptually different from merely taking one Schur-complement step?
questions.answer:
For fixed $p$, the optimal linear variables are
$$\ell^*(p)=A(p)^\dagger b.$$
Substitution gives the reduced objective
$$E_{\mathrm{red}}(p)=\|A(p)A(p)^\dagger b-b\|^2=\|\big(I-A(p)A(p)^\dagger\big)b\|^2,$$
so the outer optimisation is only
$$p^*=\arg\min_p E_{\mathrm{red}}(p),\qquad \ell^*=\ell^*(p^*).$$
In projective bundle adjustment, homogeneous landmarks can be the linear block, so every candidate set of cameras gets its best possible structure in closed form. This reduces the search space and permits optimisation from much poorer or even arbitrary initial structure, which motivates initialization-free variable-projection methods such as PoVar.
A Schur complement eliminates the landmark **increment inside one linearised Gauss–Newton system**. Variable projection eliminates the landmark variables in the **objective itself** before the outer nonlinear optimisation; the optimum structure is recomputed as a function of the current poses.
questions.extend: Both methods eliminate landmarks, but at different levels: variable projection acts on the separable objective; Schur acts on one local normal equation.

questions.q:
For monocular BA:

1. Identify the global gauge freedoms. (3)
2. Give two valid ways to remove them. (2)
3. Compare optimizing depths plus poses with optimizing explicit 3D landmarks plus poses; state one advantage of each. (3)
questions.answer: Monocular bundle adjustment has a seven-dimensional global similarity gauge: three rotations, three translations, and one scale. One may fix the first camera pose and one distance or baseline, or impose equivalent anchor/gauge priors with an explicit scale constraint. Depth-plus-pose variables are compact and naturally tied to observation rays, which is useful in two-view or inverse-depth formulations. Explicit 3D landmarks are more symmetric across many views and fit the standard sparse bundle-adjustment structure.
questions.extend: Generated set Q46-B: Gauge fixing and parameterization (8 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Which objective does the linear eight-point algorithm minimise?

options.text: Photometric intensity error
Geometric reprojection error
Neither of the above; it minimises an algebraic epipolar residual

questions.answer: The eight-point algorithm minimises an **algebraic** residual of the epipolar equations (subject to a normalisation/scale constraint), not photometric error and not the geometric reprojection error. Bundle adjustment is the subsequent method that directly minimises reprojection error.

questions.q: For two calibrated views with 3D points $X_j$ in camera 1, observations $\tilde x_i^j$, relative pose $(R,T)$ and projection $\pi$, state the bundle-adjustment cost and its main advantage over the eight-point algorithm given a good initialisation.
questions.answer: The two-view cost is $E(R,T,X_1,\ldots,X_N)=\sum_{j=1}^N\big(\|\tilde x_1^j-\pi(X_j)\|^2+\|\tilde x_2^j-\pi(RX_j+T)\|^2\big)$. Its main advantage is that nonlinear least squares optimises the physically meaningful reprojection error jointly over pose and structure and can incorporate robust losses, so with a good initialisation it is more accurate and less sensitive to noise/outliers than the linear eight-point estimate.

knowledge_points.title: The Schur Complement and Marginalising Landmarks
knowledge_points.recap:
**The normal equations in block form.** Splitting the unknowns into cameras $\Delta x_p$ and landmarks $\Delta x_\ell$,
$$\begin{pmatrix}U&W\\W^\top&V\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x_p\\\Delta x_\ell\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b_p\\b_\ell\end{pmatrix},$$
with $U=J_p^\top J_p+\lambda D_p^\top D_p$, $W=J_p^\top J_\ell$, $V=J_\ell^\top J_\ell+\lambda D_\ell^\top D_\ell$, $b_p=-J_p^\top r$, $b_\ell=-J_\ell^\top r$.
**Eliminate the landmarks.** From the second block row, $\Delta x_\ell=V^{-1}(b_\ell-W^\top\Delta x_p)$. Substituting into the first gives the **reduced camera system**
$$\underbrace{\big(U-WV^{-1}W^\top\big)}_{S:\ \text{Schur complement}}\Delta x_p=b_p-WV^{-1}b_\ell.$$
**Why landmarks and not cameras.** $V$ is **block-diagonal** with tiny $3\times3$ blocks (one per landmark), so $V^{-1}$ is obtained by inverting each block independently — trivially cheap and parallel. $U$ is not block-diagonal (cameras are coupled through shared landmarks), so eliminating cameras would require a genuinely large inverse. Moreover there are typically far more landmarks than cameras, so $S$ (size = number of camera parameters) is *much* smaller than the full system.
**Power-series / iterative Schur.** For $\|M\|<1$ the geometric series gives $(I-M)^{-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{m}M^i+R$ with $R\to0$. Writing $S=C_0-E_S$ with $C_0$ the **block-diagonal** part of $C$ and $E_S=C_0-S$:
$$S=C_0\big(I-C_0^{-1}E_S\big)\ \Longrightarrow\ S^{-1}=\big(I-C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^{-1}C_0^{-1}\approx\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^iC_0^{-1}=:\hat S(m).$$
**Convergence condition:** $\|C_0^{-1}E_S\|<1$. **Why $C_0$:** being block-diagonal it is far faster to invert than $C$ itself. **Error:** $P(m)=S^{-1}-\hat S(m)$ satisfies $SP(m)=\big(E_SC_0^{-1}\big)^{m+1}$, which decays geometrically.

questions.q: For the damped normal equations $\begin{pmatrix}U&W\\W^\top&V\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x_p\\\Delta x_\ell\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}b_p\\b_\ell\end{pmatrix}$: (a) identify $U,W,V,b_p,b_\ell$ in terms of $J_p,J_\ell,r,\lambda,D$; (b) eliminate $\Delta x_\ell$ and derive the Schur complement system; (c) what are the dimensions of $S$, and why is inverting $V$ cheap? (d) Why do we eliminate landmarks rather than cameras?
questions.answer:
**(a)** $U=J_p^\top J_p+\lambda D_p^\top D_p$, $W=J_p^\top J_\ell$, $V=J_\ell^\top J_\ell+\lambda D_\ell^\top D_\ell$, $b_p=-J_p^\top r$, $b_\ell=-J_\ell^\top r$.
**(b)** The second block row gives $W^\top\Delta x_p+V\Delta x_\ell=b_\ell$, i.e. $\Delta x_\ell=V^{-1}\big(b_\ell-W^\top\Delta x_p\big)$. Substituting into the first row $U\Delta x_p+W\Delta x_\ell=b_p$:
$$\big(U-WV^{-1}W^\top\big)\Delta x_p=b_p-WV^{-1}b_\ell,$$
with $S=U-WV^{-1}W^\top$ the **Schur complement**. Solve for $\Delta x_p$, then back-substitute for $\Delta x_\ell$.
**(c)** $S$ has the size of the **camera** parameter block ($6n_c$ or $12n_c$) — far smaller than the full system. $V$ is **block-diagonal** with one small $3\times3$ block per landmark, so $V^{-1}$ is just those blocks inverted independently: $O(n_l)$ work and trivially parallel.
**(d)** Because only the landmark block is block-diagonal. Landmarks do not interact with each other directly (they are coupled only through the cameras), whereas cameras *are* coupled through shared landmarks, so $U$ is not block-diagonal and eliminating cameras would require inverting a large dense matrix. Additionally $n_l\gg n_c$ in practice, so eliminating the landmarks removes by far the most unknowns.
questions.extend: The Schur complement is exactly "marginalising out" the landmarks — the same operation appears in sliding-window SLAM when old keyframes are marginalised.

questions.q: Let $S=C-E^\top B^{-1}E$ be the Schur complement of $\begin{pmatrix}B&E\\E^\top&C\end{pmatrix}$, and let $C_0$ be the block-diagonal part of $C$, $E_S=C_0-S$. (a) Approximate $S^{-1}$ by a power series of order $m$ depending only on $C_0$ and $E_S$. (b) What condition ensures convergence? (c) Why is it useful to introduce $C_0$?
questions.answer:
**(a)** Write $S=C_0-E_S=C_0\big(I-C_0^{-1}E_S\big)$. Therefore
$$S^{-1}=\big(I-C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^{-1}C_0^{-1}\approx\hat S(m)=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^iC_0^{-1},$$
using the geometric series $(I-M)^{-1}\approx\sum_{i=0}^{m}M^i$.
**(b)** Convergence requires
$$\big\|C_0^{-1}E_S\big\|<1.$$
**(c)** Because $C_0$ is **block-diagonal**, it is much faster to invert than $C$ (or than $S$ itself): each small diagonal block is inverted independently. The power series then replaces one expensive inverse with a few cheap block inversions and matrix–vector products — the basis of the "power Schur complement" / iterative Schur solvers used in large-scale bundle adjustment.
questions.extend: Same idea as a preconditioned iterative solve: $C_0^{-1}$ is the preconditioner, and $m$ trades accuracy against cost.

questions.q: Let $P(m)=S^{-1}-\hat S(m)$ be the error induced by the power-series approximation. Find the matrix $A$ and the scalar $l$ such that $SP(m)=A^l$.
questions.answer:
$$SP(m)=\big(E_SC_0^{-1}\big)^{m+1},$$
so $A=E_SC_0^{-1}$ and $l=m+1$.
**Derivation.**
$$SP(m)=I-S\hat S(m)=I-(C_0-E_S)\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^iC_0^{-1}$$
$$=I-C_0\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^iC_0^{-1}+E_S\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(C_0^{-1}E_S\big)^iC_0^{-1}$$
$$=I-\sum_{i=0}^{m}\big(E_SC_0^{-1}\big)^i+\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\big(E_SC_0^{-1}\big)^i=\big(E_SC_0^{-1}\big)^{m+1},$$
since the two sums telescope, leaving only the last term of the second minus the first term ($I$) of the first.
**Reading.** The error decays like the $(m{+}1)$-st power of $E_SC_0^{-1}$ — geometric convergence, provided the norm condition $\|C_0^{-1}E_S\|<1$ holds.
questions.extend: The telescoping trick — pushing $C_0$ through $(C_0^{-1}E_S)^i$ to turn it into $(E_SC_0^{-1})^i$ — is the whole computation.

questions.q:
There are $n_p$ cameras with $d_p$ parameters, $n_\ell$ 3D landmarks, and $n_{obs}$ image observations, each producing a 2D residual.

1. Give the dimensions of $J_p$, $J_\ell$, and $J=[J_p\ J_\ell]$. (3)
2. Describe exactly which blocks in one residual row can be nonzero. (3)
3. Explain why $J_\ell^\top J_\ell$ is block diagonal. (2)
questions.answer:
The dimensions are
$$J_p\in\mathbb R^{2n_{obs}\times d_pn_p},\qquad J_\ell\in\mathbb R^{2n_{obs}\times3n_\ell},$$
$$J=[J_p\ J_\ell]\in\mathbb R^{2n_{obs}\times(d_pn_p+3n_\ell)}.$$
One 2D observation depends only on its camera and landmark, so exactly those two parameter blocks can be non-zero in its residual rows. Distinct landmarks never occur in the same residual; therefore $J_\ell^\top J_\ell$ is block diagonal with one $3\times3$ block per landmark.
questions.extend: Generated set Q49-A: Dimensions and sparsity pattern (8 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.
tags: BA Jacobian sparsity and the Schur complement

questions.q:
Given

$$
\begin{bmatrix}U&W\\W^\top&V\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_p\\\Delta x_\ell\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}b_p\\b_\ell\end{bmatrix},
$$

derive the reduced camera system and the landmark back-substitution. State the dimensions of the Schur complement and explain why landmarks, rather than cameras, are normally eliminated. (10)
questions.answer:
Eliminating $\Delta x_\ell$ gives
$$S=U-WV^{-1}W^\top,$$
$$S\Delta x_p=b_p-WV^{-1}b_\ell.$$
After solving the reduced camera system, back-substitute
$$\Delta x_\ell=V^{-1}(b_\ell-W^\top\Delta x_p).$$
The Schur complement has size $d_pn_p\times d_pn_p$. Landmarks are eliminated because $V$ consists of many small independent blocks whose inverses are cheap, and there are usually far more landmarks than cameras.
questions.extend: Generated set Q49-B: Eliminating landmarks (10 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.

knowledge_points.title: Constrained Optimisation Identities and Projected Gradient Descent
knowledge_points.recap:
**The Rayleigh identity, reused constantly.** For a symmetric $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$:
$$\min_{\|x\|=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle=\lambda_n,\qquad \max_{\|x\|=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle=\lambda_1,$$
attained at the corresponding unit eigenvectors. Two consequences the exam uses repeatedly:
$\bullet$ On the unit sphere $\langle x,x\rangle=1$, so any additive $c\langle x,x\rangle$ term is a **constant** $c$: $\min_{\|x\|=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle+5\langle x,x\rangle=\lambda_n+5$.
$\bullet$ Minimising $-\langle x,Ax\rangle$ maximises $\langle x,Ax\rangle$, so the minimiser is the eigenvector of the **largest** eigenvalue and the value is $-\lambda_1$.
**Newton on a quadratic.** For $f(x)=\langle x,(A+cI)x\rangle$: $\nabla f=2(A+cI)x$, $H=2(A+cI)$. If $A+cI$ has no zero eigenvalue it is invertible, so Newton always applies, and the step with size $t$ is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-tH^{-1}\nabla f=x_k-t\big(2(A+cI)\big)^{-1}2(A+cI)x_k=(1-t)x_k.$$
With $t=1$ it converges in **one** step, as it must on a quadratic.
**Projected gradient descent.** For $\min_{x\in\mathcal{C}}f(x)$ alternate a gradient step and a projection:
$$x_l=x_k-\tau\nabla f(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\|x_l-x\|_2^2.$$
For the interval constraint $\|x\|_2^2\le4$ in $\mathbb{R}$ the projection is simply clamping:
$$x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}2&x_l>2\\-2&x_l<-2\\x_l&|x_l|\le2\end{cases}$$
The same pattern reappears throughout the course: project onto $O(n)$/$SO(n)$ with the SVD (Ch. 1), project onto the essential space (Ch. 5), clamp onto a box here.

questions.q: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues $0.9=\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n=0.2$. What is the value of $a^\star=\min_{\|x\|_2=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle+5\langle x,x\rangle$?
questions.answer:
$a^\star=5.2$.
**Computation.** On the unit sphere $\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2=1$, so the second term is the constant $5$:
$$a^\star=\min_{\|x\|=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle+5=\lambda_n+5=0.2+5=5.2,$$
using $\min_{\|x\|=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle=\lambda_{\min}$ (Rayleigh quotient).
questions.extend: First simplify with $\|x\|=1$, then apply the Rayleigh bound. Almost every "optimisation" MC on these papers is this two-step move.

options.text: The given information is insufficient

questions.q: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues ordered $0.6=\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n=0.4$. What is the value of $a^\star=\min_{\|x\|=1}\langle3x,-Ax+x\rangle$?
questions.answer:
$a^\star=1.2$.
**Computation.** Expand: $\langle3x,-Ax+x\rangle=3\big(-\langle x,Ax\rangle+\langle x,x\rangle\big)=3\big(1-\langle x,Ax\rangle\big)$ on the unit sphere. Minimising this means **maximising** $\langle x,Ax\rangle$, whose maximum is the **largest** eigenvalue $\lambda_1=0.6$. Hence
$$a^\star=3(1-0.6)=3\cdot0.4=1.2.$$
questions.extend: The minus sign flips min into max — so it is $\lambda_{\max}$ here, not $\lambda_{\min}$. That flip is the entire question.

options.text: None of the other values

questions.q: For $A$ symmetric with eigenvalues $0.9=\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n=0.2$: (a) can Newton's method always be applied to $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\langle x,Ax\rangle+5\langle x,x\rangle$? Write the update step with step size $t$. (b) What is the solution of $x^\star=\arg\min_{\|x\|_2=1}\langle x,x\rangle-\langle x,Ax\rangle$ in terms of eigenvectors of $A$, and (c) the value of the objective at $x^\star$?
questions.answer:
**(a)** Rewrite the objective as $\langle x,(A+5I)x\rangle$. Its gradient is $g=2(A+5I)x$ and its Hessian $H=2(A+5I)$. Since $A+5I$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $\lambda_i+5\in[5.2,5.9]$, all non-zero, it is **invertible** — so Newton's method can always be applied. The update:
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-tH^{-1}g=x_k-t\big(2(A+5I)\big)^{-1}2(A+5I)x_k=(1-t)x_k.$$
**(b)** On the unit sphere $\langle x,x\rangle=1$, so $\arg\min_{\|x\|=1}\big(1-\langle x,Ax\rangle\big)=\arg\min_{\|x\|=1}-\langle x,Ax\rangle=\arg\max_{\|x\|=1}\langle x,Ax\rangle$. The minimiser is therefore the **eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue of $A$** (equivalently, the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue of $-A$).
**(c)** The value is $1-\lambda_1=1-0.9=0.1$.
questions.extend: With $t=1$ the Newton update gives $x_1=0$ — the exact minimiser of the (positive definite) quadratic in a single step, as expected.

questions.q: For $x^\star=\arg\min_{\|x\|_2^2\le4,\ x\in\mathbb{R}}f(x)$ with $f(x)=-\cos(8x)e^{-4x^2}$, projected gradient descent alternates $x_l=x_k-\tau\nabla f(x_k)$ and $x_{k+1}=\arg\min_{\|x\|_2^2\le4}\|x_l-x\|_2^2$. Write down both update steps explicitly.
questions.answer:
**Gradient step.** Differentiating $f(x)=-\cos(8x)e^{-4x^2}$ by the product rule gives $\nabla f(x)=8e^{-4x^2}\big(\sin(8x)+x\cos(8x)\big)$, hence
$$x_l=x_k-8\tau e^{-4x_k^2}\big(\cos(8x_k)\,x_k+\sin(8x_k)\big).$$
**Projection step.** The constraint $\|x\|_2^2\le4$ is the interval $[-2,2]$, and the Euclidean projection onto it is a clamp:
$$x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}2&\text{if }x_l>2\\-2&\text{if }x_l<-2\\x_l&\text{if }|x_l|\le2.\end{cases}$$
questions.extend: Projected gradient descent = unconstrained step, then the nearest point of the feasible set. The projection is the only place the constraint enters.

questions.q: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with eigenvalues ordered $0.8=\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n=0.4$. What is the value of $a^\star=\min_{\|x\|=1}\langle2x,-Ax+x\rangle$?
questions.answer:
$a^\star=0.4$.
**Computation.** Expand on the unit sphere, where $\langle x,x\rangle=1$:
$$\langle2x,-Ax+x\rangle=2\big(-\langle x,Ax\rangle+\langle x,x\rangle\big)=2\big(1-\langle x,Ax\rangle\big).$$
Minimising this means **maximising** $\langle x,Ax\rangle$, whose maximum is $\lambda_1=0.8$. Hence
$$a^\star=2(1-0.8)=2\cdot0.2=0.4.$$
questions.extend: The same template appears in three different papers: pull out the constant from $\|x\|=1$, watch the sign, then read off $\lambda_{\max}$ or $\lambda_{\min}$.

options.text: None of the other values

questions.q: For projected gradient descent on the Euclidean ball $\mathcal C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n\mid\|x\|_2\le r\}$, derive the projection $\Pi_{\mathcal C}(y)$. Then write one complete iteration for a differentiable objective $f$ and explain why normalizing every iterate to norm $r$ is wrong.
questions.answer:
If $\|y\|\le r$, the closest feasible point is $y$. Otherwise the KKT conditions show that the closest point lies on the same ray with norm $r$. Hence
$$\Pi_{\mathcal C}(y)=\begin{cases}y,&\|y\|\le r,\\r\,y/\|y\|,&\|y\|>r.\end{cases}$$
One iteration is
$$y_k=x_k-\tau\nabla f(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal C}(y_k).$$
Always normalizing to norm $r$ projects onto the sphere, not the ball, and incorrectly moves feasible interior points to the boundary.
questions.extend: Cremers-style coverage question; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Let $A=A^\top$ and consider $\min_{\|x\|=1}x^\top Ax$. Derive the stationarity equation with a Lagrange multiplier, identify all stationary values, and explain why taking an unconstrained Newton step on $x^\top Ax$ cannot solve the constrained problem.
questions.answer:
With
$$L(x,\lambda)=x^\top Ax-\lambda(x^\top x-1),$$
stationarity gives
$$2Ax-2\lambda x=0,$$
so every stationary point is a unit eigenvector and its objective value is the corresponding eigenvalue. The global minimum is attained in the eigenspace of $\lambda_{\min}(A)$. Unconstrained Newton minimizes the quadratic over all of $\mathbb R^n$ and ignores feasibility; for a positive-definite $A$ it moves to $x=0$, which violates $\|x\|=1$. The constraint must be enforced by a manifold, multiplier, or projection method.
